blocks.text: A turner machining a medium-carbon steel shaft sees a long, curled, shiny-backed ribbon leave the tool, and a motor ammeter that jumps as the cut starts. Both are readouts of one small event: a thin zone of metal in front of the tool shearing. By measuring how thick the chip is and how hard the tool is pushed, an engineer can infer the shear angle, the friction on the tool face and the energy that every cubic millimetre of metal costs.

blocks.markdown: In **orthogonal cutting** the cutting edge is perpendicular to the cutting velocity, so the process is two-dimensional and can be drawn in the plane of the page. The tool removes a layer of **uncut chip thickness** $t_0$ (mm), which is the feed in a simple turning set-up, across a width $w$ (mm). The workpiece material shears along a thin plane inclined at the **shear angle** $\phi$ to the cutting direction, and leaves as a chip of thickness $t_c$ (mm). The tool face is tilted by the **rake angle** $\alpha$ (positive when the face leans away from the work). The chip is almost always thicker than the layer it came from, because material is compressed and sheared as it passes the shear plane.

blocks.title: Chip thickness ratio
blocks.text: The chip thickness ratio (cutting ratio) is $r = t_0 / t_c$. Because the chip is thicker than the uncut layer, $t_c > t_0$ and so $r < 1$ in ordinary machining. A small $r$ means a thick, heavily deformed chip and a low shear angle; $r$ closer to 1 means a thin, easily formed chip.

blocks.markdown: Geometry of the shear plane gives its length two ways: $t_0/\sin\phi$ from the uncut side, and $t_c/\cos(\phi-\alpha)$ from the chip side. Equating them (the chip has the same width and the same material, so volume is conserved) links the measurable ratio $r$ to the unmeasurable shear angle $\phi$. Expanding $\cos(\phi-\alpha)$ and dividing by $\cos\phi$ gives the working formula below.

blocks.caption: Shear angle from chip thickness ratio (orthogonal cutting, sharp tool, no side flow)

blocks.title: Shear angle from a measured chip
blocks.prompt: A steel is turned orthogonally with uncut thickness $t_0 = 0.25$ mm. The chip is measured as $t_c = 0.55$ mm and the tool rake angle is $\alpha = 10^\circ$. Find $r$ and the shear angle $\phi$.

steps.text: Chip thickness ratio from the two thicknesses.
Evaluate numerator and denominator with $\cos 10^\circ=0.9848$ and $\sin 10^\circ=0.1736$.

blocks.answer: r = 0.455 and the shear angle is about 25.9 degrees.

blocks.markdown: Next, forces. A **tool-post dynamometer** (a piezoelectric or strain-gauge force plate) reports two components in orthogonal cutting: the **cutting force** $F_c$ (N) along the cutting velocity and the **thrust force** $F_t$ (N) perpendicular to it. These are not the forces on the tool face. Resolving them onto the rake face gives the **friction force** $F$ along the face and the **normal force** $N$ perpendicular to it. Their ratio is the mean coefficient of friction on the face, $\mu = F/N = \tan\beta$, where $\beta$ is the **friction angle**.

blocks.latex: F = F_c\sin\alpha + F_t\cos\alpha, \qquad N = F_c\cos\alpha - F_t\sin\alpha, \qquad \mu=\frac{F}{N}=\tan\beta
blocks.caption: Rake-face friction and normal forces (positive rake angle, forces in N)

blocks.title: Friction angle from dynamometer readings
blocks.prompt: A dynamometer records $F_c = 1200$ N and $F_t = 480$ N with a tool of rake angle $\alpha=10^\circ$. Find the friction force, normal force, coefficient of friction and friction angle.

steps.text: Friction force along the rake face.
Normal force on the rake face.
Coefficient of friction and friction angle.

blocks.answer: F = 681 N, N = 1098 N, so mu = 0.62 and the friction angle is about 31.8 degrees.

rows: Feed per revolution (turning) or set by the tool
blocks.caption: Measured and derived quantities in orthogonal cutting

blocks.markdown: Forces tell you about the tool; energy tells you about the material. The power consumed at the cutting point is $P = F_c v$, with $v$ the cutting speed in m/s (the thrust force does no work because there is no motion in its direction). The **material removal rate** is the volume of metal removed per second, $\text{MRR} = v\,w\,t_0$. Dividing power by removal rate gives the **specific cutting energy** $u$, the energy needed to remove one unit volume. Since $P/\text{MRR} = F_c v/(v w t_0)$, $u = F_c/(w t_0)$, simply the cutting force divided by the uncut chip area.

blocks.caption: Specific cutting energy; with $P$ in W and MRR in mm$^3$/s, $u$ is in J/mm$^3$, and 1 J/mm$^3$ = 1000 N/mm$^2$

blocks.title: Specific cutting energy from force and from power
blocks.prompt: A cut has width $w=3$ mm, uncut thickness $t_0=0.2$ mm, cutting speed $v=90$ m/min and cutting force $F_c=1500$ N. Find the cutting power, the MRR and the specific cutting energy.

steps.text: Convert speed to m/s and find the cutting power.
Material removal rate in mm$^3$/s (speed converted to 1500 mm/s).
Divide power by MRR, then check against force over chip area.

blocks.answer: P = 2250 W, MRR = 900 mm^3/s and u = 2.50 J/mm^3 (= 2500 N/mm^2), a typical order of magnitude for a carbon steel.

blocks.title: Larger shear angle means easier cutting
blocks.text: For a given material and tool, a larger $\phi$ means a shorter shear plane, a thinner chip ($r$ nearer 1), less work of deformation and lower cutting force. Merchant's minimum-energy argument gives the typical approximation $\phi \approx 45^\circ + \alpha/2 - \beta/2$: more rake (larger $\alpha$) or less friction (smaller $\beta$) raises the shear angle. This is an idealised model; real materials deviate from it, so treat it as a guide, not a law. Also avoid sign traps: with positive rake, friction is $F = F_c\sin\alpha + F_t\cos\alpha$, not $F_c\cos\alpha + F_t\sin\alpha$, and keep speed in m/s for watts but mm/s for MRR in mm$^3$/s.

points: The chip thickness ratio $r=t_0/t_c$ and rake angle $\alpha$ give the shear angle through $\tan\phi=r\cos\alpha/(1-r\sin\alpha)$.
Dynamometer forces $F_c$ and $F_t$ resolve to rake-face friction $F=F_c\sin\alpha+F_t\cos\alpha$ and normal force $N=F_c\cos\alpha-F_t\sin\alpha$, giving $\mu=\tan\beta=F/N$.
Specific cutting energy is $u=P/\text{MRR}=F_c/(w t_0)$, a property of the work material that lets you predict power for any cut.
Larger shear angle, lower friction and more positive rake all reduce cutting force and energy.

questions.stem: In orthogonal metal cutting the chip thickness ratio is defined as $r=t_0/t_c$. For ordinary machining, which statement about $r$ is correct?

options.text: $r>1$, because the chip is thinner than the uncut layer
$r<1$, because the chip is thicker than the uncut layer

questions.correctOptionText: $r<1$, because the chip is thicker than the uncut layer

distractorRationale.a: The chip is compressed and sheared so it comes out thicker, not thinner, so $r>1$ would imply a chip thinner than the cut.
distractorRationale.c: Volume is conserved, but the chip is shorter than the cut length as well as thicker, so the thicknesses differ and $r=1$ does not follow.
distractorRationale.d: The rake angle enters the shear-angle formula but $r$ is a ratio of thicknesses, not a tangent of the rake angle.

questions.explanation: The material is compressed along the shear plane, so the chip leaving the tool is shorter and thicker than the layer cut. Since $t_c>t_0$, the ratio $r=t_0/t_c$ is below one, and a smaller $r$ signals more severe deformation.

questions.stem: A tool with $0^\circ$ rake angle produces a chip with thickness ratio $r=0.5$. What is the shear angle?

distractorRationale.b: $30^\circ$ comes from $\sin^{-1}(0.5)$, wrongly using sine instead of tangent.
distractorRationale.c: $45^\circ$ would need $r=1$, i.e. no chip thickening.

questions.explanation: With $\alpha=0^\circ$ the formula reduces to $\tan\phi=r$. So $\phi=\tan^{-1}(0.5)=26.6^\circ$, and the other options come from using the wrong trigonometric function or inverting $r$.

questions.stem: In an orthogonal turning test the uncut chip thickness is $t_0=0.20$ mm and the measured chip thickness is $t_c=0.48$ mm. The tool rake angle is $15^\circ$. Calculate the shear angle $\phi$ in degrees.
questions.explanation: The ratio is $r=0.20/0.48=0.4167$. Then $\tan\phi=r\cos15^\circ/(1-r\sin15^\circ)=0.4025/0.8922$, giving $\phi=24.3^\circ$. A positive rake angle raises the shear angle compared with zero rake for the same $r$.

questions.stem: A dynamometer reads cutting force $F_c$ and thrust force $F_t$ for a tool of positive rake angle $\alpha$. Which expression gives the friction force $F$ on the rake face?

distractorRationale.b: This swaps sine and cosine, which resolves the forces about the wrong axis.
distractorRationale.c: This is the expression for the normal force $N$ on the rake face, not the friction force.
distractorRationale.d: $F_t/F_c$ is a force ratio, not a force, and equals $\mu$ only when the rake angle is zero.

questions.explanation: Resolving $F_c$ and $F_t$ along the rake face gives $F=F_c\sin\alpha+F_t\cos\alpha$. The normal force is perpendicular to this, $N=F_c\cos\alpha-F_t\sin\alpha$, and the ratio $F/N$ is the friction coefficient.

questions.stem: A dynamometer measures $F_c=900$ N and $F_t=630$ N while cutting with a tool of rake angle $5^\circ$. Calculate the friction angle $\beta$ on the rake face in degrees.
questions.explanation: The friction force is $F=900\sin5^\circ+630\cos5^\circ=706.0$ N and the normal force is $N=900\cos5^\circ-630\sin5^\circ=841.7$ N. Then $\mu=F/N=0.839$ and $\beta=\tan^{-1}\mu=40.0^\circ$.

questions.stem: Turning is carried out at cutting speed 120 m/min with feed 0.25 mm/rev and depth of cut 2 mm. The cutting power measured at the tool is 3100 W. Taking MRR $=v f d$, calculate the specific cutting energy in J/mm$^3$.
questions.explanation: Speed is 120 m/min $=2000$ mm/s, so $\text{MRR}=2000\times0.25\times2=1000$ mm$^3$/s. Then $u=P/\text{MRR}=3100/1000=3.10$ J/mm$^3$, equal to 3100 N/mm$^2$.

questions.stem: A lathe spindle motor draws 6.0 kW at the shaft while removing metal at 1200 mm$^3$/s. The drive train is 80 percent efficient, so the cutting power at the tool is 80 percent of the motor power. What is the specific cutting energy of the work material?

distractorRationale.a: $5.0$ J/mm$^3$ uses the full motor power and ignores the drive losses, so it overstates the energy used in cutting.
distractorRationale.b: $3.2$ J/mm$^3$ applies the efficiency twice (multiplying 4.0 by 0.8 again).
distractorRationale.d: $0.8$ J/mm$^3$ is the efficiency itself, not an energy per unit volume.

questions.explanation: Cutting power is $0.80\times6000=4800$ W. Dividing by the MRR gives $u=4800/1200=4.0$ J/mm$^3$, which is the energy absorbed at the cutting zone, not including machine losses.

questions.stem: A student machines the same steel with two tools that differ only in rake angle: $0^\circ$ and $+15^\circ$. The chip from the $+15^\circ$ tool is noticeably thinner. Explain, using the shear-angle relation and the chip thickness ratio, why the chip is thinner and what happens to the cutting force.
markingGuide: States $\tan\phi=r\cos\alpha/(1-r\sin\alpha)$ or equivalent and notes that a thinner chip means larger $r=t_0/t_c$ (nearer 1)
Explains that larger rake angle tends to increase the shear angle $\phi$
Links larger $\phi$ to a shorter shear plane and less shear deformation
Concludes that the cutting force and specific energy fall with the more positive rake
Mentions a limitation, such as a weaker cutting edge or that the ideal model is approximate
questions.explanation: A more positive rake angle lets the chip flow away more easily, which raises $\phi$ and brings $r$ closer to 1, so the chip is thinner. A larger shear angle shortens the shear plane, so less metal is sheared per unit time and the cutting force falls.

questions.stem: Describe how you would obtain the specific cutting energy of a work material from (i) a dynamometer and (ii) a power meter on the machine, and explain why the two estimates normally differ. State which is more suitable for characterising the material and why.
markingGuide: (i) Dynamometer: $u=F_c/(w t_0)$, cutting force over uncut chip area
(ii) Power meter: $u=P/\text{MRR}$ where MRR $=v w t_0$ (or $vfd$ in turning)
Notes that machine power includes idling, drive and bearing losses so the power-meter value is larger unless losses are subtracted or efficiency applied
Notes the dynamometer measures only the cutting zone, and thrust force does no work
States the dynamometer value is better for the material, with justification, and units (J/mm$^3$ or N/mm$^2$)
questions.explanation: The dynamometer measures the force at the tool, so $F_c/(wt_0)$ is the energy per unit volume in the cutting zone alone. A power meter measures the electrical or spindle input, which includes losses, so unless corrected it overestimates $u$.

questions.stem: Using Merchant's relation $\phi=45^\circ+\alpha/2-\beta/2$, a tool with rake angle $\alpha=12^\circ$ cuts a material where the friction angle on the rake face is $\beta=36^\circ$. What shear angle is predicted?

distractorRationale.a: $57^\circ$ comes from adding the friction angle term instead of subtracting it.
distractorRationale.b: $45^\circ$ would result if the rake and friction terms were ignored.
distractorRationale.c: $39^\circ$ comes from subtracting only $\beta/2$ with the wrong arithmetic (dropping the $\alpha/2$ term and mis-halving).

questions.explanation: Substituting gives $\phi=45+12/2-36/2=45+6-18=33^\circ$. A higher friction angle lowers the shear angle, which raises the chip thickness and the force, so lubrication that reduces $\beta$ helps cutting.
